title: Writing Professionally
area: BCA 105 · Professional Communication and Ethics · Unit 3
html:
Writing is the permanent face of a professional: the email that closes a deal, the notice that tells 600 students about an exam change, the cover letter that gets a CV read, the memo that records an instruction.

A written message can be reread, forwarded and used as evidence, so it must be correct, clear and courteous the first time.

This unit covers the rules of professional writing, text messages, emails and memos, notices, informal and formal letters, résumés and cover letters, business vocabulary and the active and passive voice, and the two prescribed readings, "Gateman's Gift" and "My School".

What this unit gives you
  • The rules of professional writing: planning, tone, words, sentences, paragraphs and proofreading (3.1).
  • Text messages, emails and memos with models (3.2); notice writing (3.3); informal and formal letters (3.4).
  • Résumé and cover letter formats with models (3.5).
  • Business vocabulary and its uses; active and passive voice (3.6).
  • Reading notes, analysis and solved exercises for "Gateman's Gift" and "My School" (3.7).

3.1 Rules of professional writing

Professional writing is reader-centred, purposeful and economical. The reader is busy, may read only the first lines on a phone, and will act on what you write. Use the following rules as a checklist.

  1. Know your purpose and reader. Before writing, finish two sentences: "I want the reader to ___" and "The reader already knows ___." If you cannot, you are not ready to write.
  2. Put the main point first (direct approach). Good news and routine requests start with the point; bad news starts with a buffer and reason (indirect approach). Never bury the request in the last paragraph.
  3. Use the 7 Cs (Unit 1.3): clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous.
  4. Choose plain words. Prefer use to utilise, help to facilitate, about to with reference to. Avoid clichés ("please find enclosed herewith"), slang, abbreviations that the reader may not know and emotional language.
  5. Keep sentences short and varied (15 to 20 words on average); one idea per sentence; put the doer near the verb (The team fixed the bug, not The bug was fixed by the team unless the doer is unimportant).
  6. Write short paragraphs with a topic sentence first, support next, and a link or action last (three to five lines for screen reading).
  7. Use a positive, "you-attitude" tone. Write about what the reader can do or gain. "You will receive the refund within five days" is better than "We cannot process refunds sooner."
  8. Use bias-free language. Use chairperson not chairman, they for an unknown person, and avoid assumptions about age, gender, caste or disability.
  9. Design for scanning. Use headings, bullets, numbered steps, bold for key dates and white space; place tables for comparisons.
  10. Revise and proofread. Leave time between drafting and editing; check facts, numbers, names, dates, attachments, spelling and punctuation; read aloud; use a spell-checker but also a human eye (their/there, its/it's).

Common wordiness and its fixes

Wordy Better
due to the fact that because
at this point in time now
in the event that if
in spite of the fact that although
a large number of many
make a decision decide
it is requested that you please
with regard to / in respect of about
we are in receipt of we have received
for the purpose of for / to

The writing process

Plan (purpose, reader, outline) → Draft (get ideas down; do not edit yet) → Revise (structure, content, tone) → Edit (grammar, style, words) → Proofread (typos, format) → Send / publish and follow up.

Positive and negative wording

Negative: "You did not fill in the form correctly, so we cannot proceed." Positive: "Please correct the date of birth on the form (line 4) so that we can complete your application today."

3.2 Text messages, emails and memos

Text messages and chat (SMS, WhatsApp, Viber, Teams)

Short messages are fast and informal, but at work they are still business records.

Rules: greet and sign off briefly, state the point in the first line, use full words for first-time contacts and seniors, avoid slang and emojis with clients, do not send sensitive data (passwords, salary, health), do not message late at night unless urgent, and take serious discussions to a call or email.

Use the group chat for the group's business only; reply-all etiquette applies. Always re-read before you send; a text cannot be recalled in many apps.

Email

An email is the standard written channel in business. Its parts and good practice:

Part Good practice
To / Cc / Bcc To for people who must act; Cc for people who need to know; Bcc to protect addresses of large groups; do not "reply all" unless all need the answer
Subject line specific, 5 to 8 words, includes action or date: "Approval needed: server budget by Fri 21 Mar"
Salutation "Dear Mr Sharma," (formal); "Hello Sita," (known colleague); never "Hi guys" to a client
Opening purpose in the first two lines; thanks or context if replying
Body short paragraphs or bullets; one request per paragraph; dates and numbers in bold
Closing a clear next step ("Please reply by Thursday"), thanks, then Regards / Sincerely
Signature name, designation, organisation, phone; no long disclaimers or images
Attachments mention them in the text and attach before writing "Please find attached"; name files clearly (Invoice_0314.pdf); compress large files

Netiquette for email: reply within 24 hours (or acknowledge); do not write in capitals (it is shouting); avoid sarcasm and jokes that can be misread; do not forward private emails without permission; keep the chain history clean; proofread; never write in anger (use a 10-minute rule); remember that email is not private and can be used as evidence.

Model email: a request for a deadline extension

To: Mr Rajan Karki · Cc: Ms Mina Thapa Subject: Request: two-day extension for the SRS document (due Fri 14 Mar)

Dear Mr Karki,

I am writing to request a two-day extension for the Software Requirements Specification, now due on Friday 14 March.

The client sent revised payment-module requirements on Tuesday. Including them will make the document more accurate and avoid rework in design. With the extension, I will send the final version by Sunday 16 March, 5 pm.

Sections 1 to 4 are complete and are attached for your early review.

Please let me know if this arrangement is acceptable.

Regards, Anita Shrestha Business Analyst, Himalaya Software · 9800000000

Email types: inquiry (ask for information), request, reply/confirmation, complaint, apology, follow-up, cover email (with an attachment) and announcement.

A complaint states the facts (order number, date), the effect, and the remedy you want, without anger; an apology accepts responsibility, states the correction and prevents recurrence.

Memos

A memorandum (memo) is a short internal document used to give instructions, announce policies, request action or record decisions. It is more formal than an email, has no salutation or closing and is kept in files.

Format: organisation name and the word MEMO; To, From, Date, Subject (and Cc); a body in three parts (purpose, details, action); initials instead of a signature.

Model memo

HIMALAYA SOFTWARE PVT. LTD. MEMORANDUM To: All Software Engineers From: Rajan Karki, Head of Engineering Date: 10 March 2025 Subject: Mandatory code review before merging

Effective Monday 17 March 2025, every pull request must be reviewed and approved by at least one other engineer before it is merged into the main branch.

This step will reduce production defects, which rose by 18 per cent last quarter, and will help share knowledge across teams. Reviews should be completed within one working day; urgent fixes may be reviewed after merging with the Head of Engineering's approval.

Please read the attached guidelines and confirm by email by Friday 14 March. Contact me for questions. RK

Email Memo Letter
Audience internal or external internal usually external
Formality medium formal-neutral most formal
Format subject, salutation To/From/Date/Subject address, salutation, close
Record digital filed paper or digital paper or PDF
Speed very fast fast slowest

3.3 Notice writing

A notice is a brief public announcement displayed on a board, website or app to inform a group about an event, change or rule. It is written for people who will glance at it, so it must be short (about 50 words), specific and complete.

Format: (1) name of the organisation or issuer at the top; (2) the word NOTICE in capitals; (3) date; (4) a short heading stating the subject; (5) body with the what, when, where, who and any action or condition; (6) name, designation and signature of the issuer; (7) contact if needed.

Use the future tense or present tense ("will be held"), the passive voice for the event and the active voice for instructions, and do not use "I" or "we".

Model notice 1: event

TRIBHUVAN COLLEGE OF SCIENCE · BCA DEPARTMENT NOTICE Date: 12 March 2025 Inter-College Programming Contest All BCA students are informed that an inter-college programming contest will be held in Computer Lab 3 on Friday, 21 March 2025, from 10 am to 2 pm.

Teams of three may register with Ms R. Thapa (Room 204) by Tuesday, 18 March. A registration fee of Rs 150 per team will be collected. Certificates will be given to all participants. Sunita Rai, Coordinator

Model notice 2: change of schedule

NOTICE · 5 March 2025 · Postponement of the Semester I Internal Test The internal test of BCA 105 Professional Communication and Ethics, scheduled for 8 March 2025, is postponed to Monday, 10 March 2025, 11 am, because of the public holiday.

The venue and syllabus remain unchanged. Examination Section

Types: event notices (seminar, contest, picnic), schedule changes, exam and result notices, lost-and-found, vacancy notices, safety and IT notices (a server downtime announcement for staff: date, hours, systems affected, alternative).

Notice vs advertisement vs circular: a notice informs about something that is happening; an advertisement sells or promotes; a circular is a notice copied to many people and is usually repeated.

3.4 Informal and formal letters

Informal (personal) letters

Written to relatives, friends and close colleagues in a warm, conversational tone.

Format: sender's address and date (top right); salutation (Dear Sita); an opening that greets and responds; body in short paragraphs; closing (With love, Yours, Take care); name. Contractions and everyday language are allowed.

Use for congratulating, thanking, inviting, sympathising, or describing an experience.

Informal letter (inviting a friend)

Kathmandu, 6 March 2025

Dear Binod,

How are you? I was very happy to hear that you cleared the entrance test. Congratulations! Now my news: our college is organising a tech fest on 22 March and I will be showing my attendance app.

I would love you to come and stay for the weekend. We can visit Patan Durbar Square and then try my project together.

Please write soon and tell me your train time. My mother sends her love to your family.

Yours affectionately, Anil

Formal (business) letters

A formal letter is a business or official communication to a person or organisation outside your close circle, in a polite, impersonal style.

It follows a set layout and is used for inquiry, order, complaint, application, request, recommendation, resignation and acceptance.

Part Content
1. Letterhead / sender's address organisation's name, address, phone, email, logo
2. Date 12 March 2025 (month in words)
3. Reference number (optional) Ref: HS/HR/2025/031
4. Inside address receiver's name, designation, organisation, address
5. Salutation Dear Sir/Madam, or Dear Mr Karki (use the name if known)
6. Subject line bold, short: "Subject: Request for a demonstration of the HR software"
7. Body opening (purpose), middle (details, reasons, evidence), closing (action, thanks)
8. Complimentary close Yours faithfully (to Dear Sir/Madam), Yours sincerely (to a named person)
9. Signature block signature, printed name, designation
10. Enclosures / cc Encl.: CV, certificates; cc: Principal

Layouts: block (everything flush left, no indentation; most common today), semi-block (date and close at the right; paragraphs may be indented), and indented. Tone: polite, positive, specific; avoid threats and sarcasm even in a complaint.

Model formal letter: request for a product demonstration

Himalaya Software Pvt. Ltd., Putalisadak, Kathmandu · Tel 01-4000000

12 March 2025

The Sales Manager Nepal Cloud Services Naxal, Kathmandu

Dear Sir/Madam,

Subject: Request for a demonstration of the cloud backup service

We are a software company with 45 employees and are looking for a reliable cloud backup solution. We saw your service advertised on the Kantipur website and would like to know more.

Could you please arrange an online or in-person demonstration during the week of 24 March? We would also like your price list for 2 TB, details of data centres, and your service-level guarantee for restore times.

I will be grateful for your reply by 19 March. Please contact me on 9800000000 or at hr@himalaya.example to fix a time.

Yours faithfully, (signature) Rajan Karki IT Manager

Types of formal letters and key phrases

Type Purpose and key points Useful phrases
Inquiry ask about products, services, prices "I would be grateful if you could send..."
Order request goods; give quantity, code, price, delivery, payment "Please supply the following items..."
Complaint (claim) state fault, evidence, effect and the remedy wanted "I am writing to express my concern about..."
Adjustment (reply) accept or decline the complaint, with reasons "We apologise for the inconvenience and have..."
Application apply for a job or admission (see 3.5) "I wish to apply for the post of..."
Resignation give notice, thank, offer handover "I hereby tender my resignation..."
Recommendation assess a person's skills and character "I have known Ms X for two years..."

3.5 Resumes and cover letters

Résumé

A résumé (or CV, curriculum vitae) is a one-to-two-page summary of your education, skills, experience and achievements, designed to win an interview.

It is read for six to ten seconds at first, so it must be clean, accurate and tailored to the job. In Nepal "CV" is commonly used for both; in the USA a résumé is short (one page) and a CV is a detailed academic record.

Formats: reverse-chronological (latest first; the standard), functional (skills first; for gaps and career changes) and combination. Sections in order:

  1. Contact information: name (large), phone, professional email, city, LinkedIn or GitHub link. No photo or date of birth unless the employer asks (common in Nepal; follow the advertisement).
  2. Career objective or professional summary: two lines tailored to the job.
  3. Education: degree, institution, years, result (CGPA/percentage), relevant courses.
  4. Skills: technical (languages, tools, databases) and soft skills with proof.
  5. Projects and experience: role, organisation, dates, 2 to 4 action-verb bullets with measurable results ("Reduced report time by 40% by..."). Internships and volunteering count.
  6. Achievements, certifications, training.
  7. Extra-curricular activities and languages.
  8. References: two, with their permission, or "available on request".

Do: use action verbs (developed, designed, led, tested, reduced), keep to one page for a fresher, use one clean font, save as PDF named Anita_Shrestha_CV.pdf, proofread twice.

Do not: lie (it is cause for dismissal later), use fancy graphics that confuse applicant-tracking systems, list every school subject or write long paragraphs.

Model résumé (fresher)

ANITA SHRESTHA Kathmandu, Nepal · 9800000000 · anita.shrestha@example.com · github.com/anita-sh Objective: Motivated BCA graduate seeking a junior web-developer role where I can apply my skills in Java, SQL and clean documentation.

Education Bachelor of Computer Application (BCA), Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu College of Science · 2022–2026 · CGPA 3.62/4.00 (expected) +2 Science (Computer), Himalaya Secondary School · 2020–2022 · 3.7 GPA Skills: Java, C, SQL (MySQL), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Git; teamwork, technical writing, public speaking Projects College Library System (Java, MySQL, 2025): built a desktop app for 600 members; reduced book-issue time from three minutes to under thirty seconds; wrote the user manual.

Attendance App (Android, 2024): designed screens and database for 8 classes; presented at college tech fest. Experience: Intern, Himalaya Software (6 weeks, 2025): fixed 12 front-end bugs and wrote test cases for the payment module.

Achievements: Winner, inter-college quiz 2024; Google IT Support certificate (2024). Languages: Nepali, English, Hindi. References: available on request.

Cover letter (letter of application)

A cover letter accompanies the résumé and explains why you are the right person for this job.

It is addressed to a named person if possible, is one page (3 to 4 paragraphs), and does not repeat the CV but picks the two or three strongest matches with the job and proves them.

Structure: (1) Opening: the post applied for, where you saw it, and a one-line hook. (2) Why you: two achievements or skills matched to the advertisement's requirements, with evidence. (3) Why them: your interest in the organisation.

(4) Closing: request for an interview, availability, thanks, enclosures.

Model cover letter

Kathmandu, 12 March 2025

The Human Resource Manager Himalaya Software Pvt. Ltd., Putalisadak, Kathmandu

Dear Sir/Madam,

Subject: Application for the post of Junior Software Developer (advertised in Kantipur, 9 March 2025)

I wish to apply for the post of Junior Software Developer. I am a BCA graduate with experience in Java and SQL and a record of delivering projects that people use.

My College Library System, written in Java and MySQL, is used by 600 students and cut book-issue time by more than 80 per cent; I also documented it with a user manual and tests.

During a six-week internship at a Kathmandu start-up, I fixed twelve front-end bugs and learnt to work in a Git-based team. These experiences match your requirement for strong fundamentals and good documentation.

Your company's work on payment solutions interests me because it combines security with usability, which I studied in my final-year project. I am eager to learn from your engineers.

I have enclosed my résumé and certificates and would welcome an interview at your convenience. Thank you for your time.

Yours faithfully, Anita Shrestha Encl.: résumé, certificates

Job application checklist: read the advertisement and mirror its keywords honestly; same name, email and date across all documents; mention the post in the subject; attach documents in PDF; follow the instructions (email, hard copy, portal); prepare for the interview afterwards (2.5).

Exercise (Sections 3.1 to 3.5)

  1. State eight rules of professional writing with an example for each of two.
  2. Rewrite in plain English:(a) "In view of the fact that the server is down, kindly effectuate the utilisation of the alternate system."(b) "It is requested that the undersigned be apprised at the earliest."
  3. Write an email to your teacher requesting a meeting about your project proposal.
  4. Differentiate between an email, a memo and a formal letter in a table.
  5. Draft a notice for the BCA Society announcing a seminar on "Cyber Safety" on 28 March, 2 pm, in the college hall.
  6. Write a formal letter to a computer vendor complaining that three of the ten keyboards you ordered (order no. 417) were defective, and asking for replacements.
  7. Write the parts of a good résumé and explain the difference between a résumé and a cover letter.
  8. Prepare your own résumé and a cover letter for the post of Network Assistant advertised by Nepal Telecom.
  9. Distinguish the direct and indirect approach with an example of each.
  10. Write a memo to all staff announcing a Wi-Fi password change.
Answers and worked solutions

1. The ten rules in 3.1 (purpose and reader; main point first; 7 Cs; plain words; short sentences; short paragraphs; positive tone; bias-free language; scanning design; revision). Example: Concrete: "Submit by Friday 5 pm" not "soon". Plain words: "use" for "utilise".

2.(a) "Because the server is down, please use the alternate system."(b) "Please inform me as soon as possible."

3. Use the model in 3.2: specific subject ("Request for a 15-minute meeting on the project proposal"), purpose in the first line, two possible times, thanks, signature with roll number and class.

4. See the comparison table at the end of 3.2: audience, formality, format, record, speed.

5. Notice format of 3.3: college name, NOTICE, date, heading "Seminar on Cyber Safety", the details (date, time, venue, speaker, who may attend, registration), name and designation of the issuer, in about 50 words.

6. Follow the model in 3.4: sender's and receiver's address, date, subject "Complaint regarding defective keyboards (Order no. 417)", facts (ordered 10, received on 5 March, three keys not working), request for replacement within seven days, enclose invoice copy, Yours faithfully.

7. Parts: contact, objective, education, skills, projects and experience, achievements, references. A résumé is a factual summary of your history; a cover letter is a persuasive letter explaining why your history fits this job.

8. Use the models in 3.5 with the details of the post (networking skills, a CCNA course, a lab project).

9. Direct: begins with the main point (routine requests, good news): "Please approve the leave from 3 to 5 April." Indirect: begins with context and reasons before bad news: "We have reviewed all applications carefully... we regret that we cannot offer you the post at this time."

10. Use the memo format: To: All staff; From: IT Manager; Date; Subject: Wi-Fi password change; body: from Monday the password changes; collect the new password from the IT room; the old one stops working at 6 pm; contact IT for help.

3.6 Vocabulary and grammar

3.6.1 Business vocabulary and its uses

Word Meaning Use in a sentence
invoice a bill listing goods or services and the amount due Please pay the invoice within 30 days.
quotation (quote) a seller's statement of the price for stated goods We received three quotations for the laptops.
tender a formal offer to supply goods or do work at a price The college invited tenders for the new network.
procurement the process of obtaining goods or services The procurement of servers took two months.
stakeholder a person or group with an interest in a project Clients and users are key stakeholders.
deadline the time by which work must be finished The deadline for the report is Friday.
deliverable a product or result to be handed over The first deliverable is the design document.
agenda list of items for a meeting Please add this to the agenda.
revenue / profit / turnover income / income minus cost / total sales Revenue rose 12% but profit fell.
budget a plan of income and spending The project budget is Rs 5 lakh.
liability a legal responsibility or debt The company accepts no liability for data loss.
warranty / guarantee a promise to repair or replace The laptop has a two-year warranty.
commission a payment based on sales Agents earn a 5% commission.
retainer a fee paid in advance to secure services The firm keeps a lawyer on retainer.
outsource give work to an outside company We outsource our payroll.
negotiate discuss to reach an agreement They negotiated a lower price.
merger / acquisition joining of firms / one firm buying another The acquisition was completed in March.
consignment goods sent for sale or delivery The consignment reached Birgunj on Monday.
overdue / outstanding not paid by the due date / unpaid Please settle the outstanding balance.
brief / briefing short instruction / giving instructions The manager briefed the team.
benchmark a standard to compare with The test results exceeded the benchmark.
scalable able to grow without loss of performance A cloud solution is scalable.
ROI (return on investment) profit gained compared with cost The ROI of the training was 30%.
KPI key performance indicator Response time is our main KPI.
SLA service-level agreement The SLA promises 99.9% uptime.

Common confusions in business English: affect (verb: influence) and effect (noun: result); cheque (payment order) and check (verify); stationary (not moving) and stationery (writing materials); principal (head, main) and principle (rule); advice (noun) and advise (verb); capital (money, city) and capitol (building); continual (repeated) and continuous (without a break); complement (complete) and compliment (praise).

Abbreviations in correspondence: ASAP, FYI, EOD, N/A, Re:, Encl., cc, PS, i.e. (that is), e.g. (for example), etc. Use them only with readers who know them.

Exercise 3.6.1

Fill in the blanks with the right word (invoice, tender, warranty, deadline, stakeholders, outsource, liability, budget): (a) The company will ___ its customer support to a call centre.

(b) Please send the ___ so that we can process payment. (c) The ___ for submitting the proposal is Friday. (d) The laptop is covered by a one-year ___.

(e) All ___ were invited to the project meeting. (f) The college has called a ___ for supplying 50 computers. (g) We cannot accept ___ for loss caused by power failure.

(h) The ___ for the website is limited to Rs 3 lakh.

Answers

(a) outsource (b) invoice (c) deadline (d) warranty (e) stakeholders (f) tender (g) liability (h) budget.

3.6.2 Voice

Voice shows whether the subject does the action (active) or receives it (passive). Active: subject + verb + object ("The administrator reset the password.").

Passive: object becomes subject + be + past participle (+ by + doer) ("The password was reset by the administrator.").

Forming the passive (tense by tense).

Tense Active Passive
Simple present The team tests the code. The code is tested by the team.
Present continuous The team is testing the code. The code is being tested.
Present perfect The team has tested the code. The code has been tested.
Simple past The team tested the code. The code was tested.
Past continuous The team was testing the code. The code was being tested.
Past perfect The team had tested the code. The code had been tested.
Simple future The team will test the code. The code will be tested.
Modal The team must test the code. The code must be tested.

Other forms.

Questions "Who wrote this program?" → "By whom was this program written?" ("Was the file saved by you?")

Imperatives "Close the door." → "Let the door be closed." / "You are requested to close the door." Two objects: "The manager gave Ram a laptop." → "Ram was given a laptop by the manager." or "A laptop was given to Ram."

When to use the passive. (1) The doer is unknown or unimportant: "The server was hacked last night." (2) The action matters more than the doer: "Minutes are sent to all members." (3) Tactful or impersonal tone, especially for bad news or in scientific and technical writing: "The deadline was missed." (4) Notices and reports: "A meeting will be held on Friday." Use the active for clear, direct and short writing, especially emails, instructions and CVs ("Developed a system..."): "We will inspect the lab" is better than "The lab will be inspected by us."

Active to passive in professional writing

Active: "The finance team will pay all invoices within 30 days." Passive: "All invoices will be paid within 30 days." Active (clearer): "We found three errors in the report." Passive (hides the doer): "Three errors were found in the report." Do not use the passive for the sake of sounding formal: "It is requested by the undersigned that..." is just "Please...".

Exercise 3.6.2

  1. Change into the passive voice:(a) The engineer is repairing the server.(b) The manager has approved the leave.(c) Who designed this logo?(d) You must submit the form by Friday.(e) They will announce the results tomorrow.(f) The students were writing a report.(g) Open the file.(h) The company gave her a promotion.
  2. Change into the active voice:(a) The email was sent by the HR department.(b) The new software will be installed by the technicians.(c) All the files have been deleted.(d) By whom was the accident reported?(e) The report is being typed.
Answers

1.(a) The server is being repaired by the engineer.(b) The leave has been approved by the manager.(c) By whom was this logo designed?(d) The form must be submitted by you by Friday.(e) The results will be announced tomorrow.(f) A report was being written by the students.(g) Let the file be opened.(h) She was given a promotion by the company. / A promotion was given to her by the company.

2.(a) The HR department sent the email.(b) The technicians will install the new software.(c) Someone has deleted all the files.(d) Who reported the accident?(e) Someone is typing the report.

3.7 Readings

Read the original in your textbook first, and check names and figures against your copy before using them in an answer.

3.7.1 "Gateman's Gift" by R.K. Narayan

The writer and the text

R.K. Narayan (Rasipuram Krishnaswami Iyer Narayanaswami, 1906 to 2001) is one of the great Indian writers in English.

Almost all his fiction is set in Malgudi, an imaginary South Indian town, and treats ordinary people with gentle irony and affection.

Famous works include Swami and Friends, The Guide (Sahitya Akademi Award, 1960) and the story collection Malgudi Days. "Gateman's Gift" is a short story of a retired gatekeeper who is terrified by an official letter.

It is a comedy of fear and misunderstanding with a quiet comment on class and power.

Summary

  1. The gateman. Govind Singh was for twenty-five years the gateman (gatekeeper) of Engladia's Insurance Company in Malgudi. A former soldier, he was proud of his khaki uniform and gave the company's British "Sahib" a smart military salute whenever the Sahib's car stopped at the gate. He was punctual, obedient and loyal, and he retired on a small pension.
  2. A new hobby. In retirement he takes up the hobby of making small clay figures and models. He does it for pleasure, and it gives him something to do after a lifetime of standing at a gate.
  3. The gifts to the accountant. Whenever he goes to the company's office to collect his pension, he leaves one of his clay models for the office accountant, who admires them. Through the accountant, the models reach the company's top officer.
  4. The registered letter. One day Govind Singh receives a registered letter from his old employer. A lifetime of fear of the Sahib and of official papers makes him certain that it brings bad news: that his pension has been stopped, or that he has offended the company by playing with clay. He cannot read English easily and dare not open it.
  5. Panic. He will not open it. He runs about the town looking for someone who can tell him what is in the letter without opening it, becoming more and more frightened and acting so oddly that people think he has lost his mind. In his confusion he even breaks street lamps and is picked up by the police.
  6. The accountant explains. On the way to the police station he meets the accountant of the company by chance. The accountant tells him what the letter contains: it is a commendation (a letter of appreciation) from the Sahib for the models, with a cheque (a reward of a hundred rupees). Govind Singh is released.
  7. The ending. Relief should have made him happy. Instead, he now decides that making clay models is not an occupation for a sane man and gives it up. The one thing that gave him pleasure and recognition ends just when it is praised.

Characters

  • Govind Singh: simple, honest, loyal and obedient; proud of his service; fearful of authority; creative without knowing it.
  • The Sahib / the company: an unseen authority; the gateman's imagination makes it terrifying, although it is kind in fact.
  • The accountant: kind and practical; he values the models and solves the mystery.
  • The townspeople and police: ordinary people who see only a madman.

Themes

  • Fear of authority and the class divide. A lifetime of obedience has taught the gateman to see every official paper as a threat.
  • Fear distorts behaviour. A sensible man behaves like a madman because of anxiety.
  • Art, recognition and self-doubt. His talent appears late and by accident; praise, ironically, makes him ashamed of it.
  • Communication. The entire problem comes from one letter that was not read: a message not decoded becomes a fear (Unit 1: decoding and feedback).
  • Insecurity of old age. The small pension is his only security.
  • Humour and pathos. The tone is light but the subject (poverty, dignity, mental health) is serious.

Critical analysis and literary devices

  • Irony: the letter he dreads contains praise and a reward (situational irony); the reader suspects this before he does (dramatic irony); he gives up the hobby at the moment of recognition.
  • Narrative voice: a gently amused third-person narrator who never mocks Govind Singh: Narayan's typical humane humour (humour with pathos).
  • Symbols: the gate (boundary between powerful inside and powerless outside), the letter (authority and unspoken communication), the clay models (creativity).
  • Structure: simple, with a mystery (what is in the letter?), rising panic, a quick explanation and a quiet, ironic close.
  • Critical views: a story of class anxiety and the marginalised; an allegory of the artist who gives up when recognised; a study of how fear is made by silence. All are valid; Narayan does not preach.
  • Link to professional communication: read your mail; do not let fear fill the gap left by silence; managers should write clear, reassuring messages so that employees do not guess the worst.

Key vocabulary

gateman, pension, registered letter, commendation, cheque, clay model, bewildered, anxiety, misunderstanding, appreciation, humble, eccentric.

Exercise: "Gateman's Gift"

  1. Who is Govind Singh and what was his job?
  2. What was his hobby after retirement and what did he do with the models?
  3. Why was he afraid of the registered letter?
  4. How did his behaviour change after receiving it?
  5. How was the mystery of the letter solved, and what did the letter contain?
  6. Why does Govind Singh give up making models at the end?
  7. Long answer: "The real hero of the story is fear." Discuss.
  8. Write a short note on the irony in the story.
Answers and worked solutions

1. A retired gateman of Engladia's Insurance Company in Malgudi, with twenty-five years of service, an ex-soldier living on a small pension.

2. He made small clay figures and models; whenever he went for his pension he left one for the office accountant.

3. It was an official registered letter from his old employer; he had spent his life in fear of authority and official papers and believed it meant bad news, perhaps loss of his pension, his only security.

4. He refused to open it, grew frightened, ran about town trying to find someone to tell him the contents without opening it, acted wildly (even breaking street lamps) and was thought mad.

5. The company's accountant met him by chance on the way to the police station and told him that the letter contained the Sahib's appreciation of the models and a cheque as a reward.

6. Once the fear passed he concluded that making clay toys was not work for a sane man; recognition made him self-conscious and ended the innocent pleasure of his art.

7. Introduction: the antagonist is not a person but fear. Body: (i) fear of authority built by years of obedience; (ii) fear stops him from reading the letter; (iii) it makes a sane man act like a lunatic and the community believes it; (iv) the cure is just information: once the letter is explained, fear vanishes. Conclusion: anxiety and silence do more harm than the thing feared, and the powerless carry authority within themselves.

8. The letter he fears is praise and reward (situational irony); the reader senses this before he does (dramatic irony); and he gives up modelling at the moment he is recognised for it.

3.7.2 "My School" by Rabindranath Tagore

The writer and the text

Rabindranath Tagore (1861 to 1941) was a Bengali poet, novelist, playwright, composer and educator, and the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1913, for Gitanjali).

He founded a school at Santiniketan in Bengal in 1901, which grew into Visva-Bharati University. "My School" is a lecture delivered in the United States (1916 to 1917) and published in the collection Personality (1917).

It is an essay of ideas that explains why he founded his school and what he believes education should be.

Summary

  1. An unlikely schoolmaster. Tagore starts by saying that he started a school when he was nearly forty, after spending most of his life writing verse. People expected something odd, "the product of daring inexperience".
  2. The origin: unhappy school days. The idea of the school was not a new theory but the memory of his own school days, which he found unhappy. He admits his sensitive temperament played a part, but says that schools in general are like factories that grind out uniform results, treating children as an average and ignoring the individual.
  3. Education cut off from life. The ordinary school snatches children from a world full of mystery, nature and personality and makes them learn information about it: "We rob the child of his earth to teach him geography, of language to teach him grammar." The child's hunger for the epic is met with a chronicle of dates.
  4. Education of sympathy. We are here to accept the world, not merely to know it. We gain power by knowledge but fullness by sympathy; the highest education makes our life in harmony with all existence. Schools ignore and even repress this education of sympathy.
  5. Children and nature. Children love life; they are not born ascetics ready for monastic discipline. In his school boys study under trees; he defends a boy who chose a fork of a branch for his studies, saying that childhood is the one time when a civilised man can choose the branch of a tree rather than a drawing-room chair.
  6. Ancient India and the teacher. In ancient India the school was where life itself was: students lived with the master, herded cattle, gathered fuel and fruit, and learnt from the teacher's own spiritual growth. Teaching was part of a teacher's life, not his profession.
  7. Simplicity, not poverty worship. He explains the plainness of his school: poverty brings a child into touch with life; wealth is "a golden cage". Bareness of furniture leads to personal experience of the world.
  8. Freedom of mind. The aim of education is the unity of truth and freedom of mind and soul; freedom has its risks and responsibilities, as life does. He wants children free from barriers of country, race and creed.
  9. Honest ending. He warns the audience not to carry away an exaggerated picture of the ashram: there are obstacles, weak faith in children's minds, and "a good number of inevitable failures."

Themes

  • Education as living, not information. Learning must be rooted in experience, nature and the whole personality.
  • Freedom versus discipline. Mechanical discipline kills joy and creativity.
  • Harmony with nature and sympathy. Knowledge should link the learner to the world, not set mind and nature in opposition.
  • Teacher as companion. The teacher teaches by life and love, not by command.
  • Simplicity of life, universal humanism. Santiniketan welcomes all cultures and rejects narrow nationalism.

Critical analysis and rhetorical notes

  • Form: a spoken lecture turned into an essay; personal, reflective, with the first person and anecdotes; moves from memory to criticism to ideal to honest caution.
  • Imagery and metaphor: school as a "manufactory", a "tailoring department" and the "shoes of a mandarin woman" that pinch (reference to foot-binding); wealth as a "golden cage"; the idea as a seed that grows into a plant, not a fixed foundation.
  • Contrast and antithesis: information versus experience, knowledge versus sympathy, drawing-room chair versus tree branch.
  • Ethos: honesty and self-deprecation; he admits his inexperience and the school's failures, which makes the argument credible. Pathos: the picture of a child's suffering "subdued at last into silence by punishment". Logos: the contrast with ancient India and the argument about the unity of mind, body and spirit.
  • Critical view: the essay is idealistic and written from the viewpoint of a privileged poet; critics note that his school was small and depended on a rare teacher. Yet many reforms he argued for (activity learning, outdoor classes, arts, no corporal punishment) are central to modern education.
  • Link to professional communication: good communication, like good education, depends on respect for the individual; a manager is also a teacher.

Key vocabulary

ashram, sympathy, harmony, ascetic, mechanical, discipline, uniform, manufactory, sensitive, bareness, primary, suppress, seclusion.

Exercise: "My School"

  1. When and why did Tagore start his school?
  2. What does Tagore compare the ordinary school to, and why?
  3. Explain: "We rob the child of his earth to teach him geography, of language to teach him grammar."
  4. What is the "education of sympathy"?
  5. Why does Tagore defend a boy who climbed a tree to study?
  6. How did the students of ancient India learn?
  7. Long answer: Discuss Tagore's ideas of the aim of education. Are they relevant to a computing student today?
  8. Write a paragraph comparing a rote-learning class with one that is activity based.
Answers and worked solutions

1. In 1901 at Santiniketan, when he was nearing forty, because of the unhappy memory of his own school days, which he found mechanical and cold, and not out of a new theory.

2. To a "manufactory" that grinds out uniform results and a "tailoring department", because it treats all children as the same average and ignores individuality and life.

3. Children are taught facts about the world (geography) and rules of language (grammar) in place of experiencing the earth and speaking living language; knowledge is separated from life.

4. Learning to live in sympathy and harmony with the world and all beings, not only gathering information; it is "fullness" as opposed to power.

5. Because childhood is the only time when a civilised person may choose a tree branch over a drawing-room chair, and a school should not take that freedom away.

6. They lived with their teachers in their homes, took the cattle to pasture, gathered fuel and fruit, and learnt through the teacher's life of aspiration.

7. Introduction: Tagore says the object of education is freedom of mind and the unity of truth. Body: (i) knowledge must connect to life and sympathy; (ii) freedom has risks, but only free learners grow; (iii) the teacher is a companion; (iv) relevance: computing students must learn by building, experimenting, and collaborating, not by cramming; creativity, ethics and empathy are as important as syntax. Conclusion: his ideals remain a standard for judging any education system.

8. Model: In a rote class the teacher dictates and students memorise; the knowledge fades after the exam. In an activity class students build a project, ask questions and teach each other. Learning is slower at first but lasts, which is what Tagore wanted.
